titel: Jane Schoenbrun on Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

faehigkeiten.grund: Dynamik weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen: keine Merkmale gefunden, aber eine unveraenderte Wiederholungsprobe beweist nichts

einzeiler: Jane Schoenbrun on Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma
kurzfassung: Jane Schoenbrun discusses their Cannes hit Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a meta-textual slasher film starring Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson. The conversation explores the connections between fear, desire, queerness, and cinematic language. Schoenbrun also reflects on moving away from the heavy dysphoria of their earlier work toward a more joyful and playful cinematic expression.

Moving from the crisis and dysphoria of World's Fair and I Saw the TV Glow to the gender euphoria of Camp Miasma

kapitel.titel: Refusing Allegory and the Trans Image

clips.hook: Avoiding the slasher genre due to gore sensitivity
clips.text: The host admits to avoiding horror movies growing up because they are easily startled by violence.

clips.hook: The pleasure of feeling fear without actual danger

clips.hook: Evasion of allegory in cinematic storytelling
clips.text: The conversation addresses the desire to loosen the strict relationship between on-screen images and direct metaphors.

clips.hook: Finding comfort in online spaces during a crisis

clips.hook: Fast production timelines and trusted collaborators

beschreibung:
Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Jane Schoenbrun’s third narrative feature, opens in theaters tomorrow. Dizzyingly meta-textual and deliciously, well, campy, the film stars Hannah Einbinder as an emerging queer filmmaker tasked with directing a reboot of a fictional ’80s slasher franchise titled Camp Miasma. She decides to visit the final girl of the original movie who is now an eccentric middle-aged recluse, played by Gillian Anderson, who’s living on the campgrounds where the first movie was shot. What unfolds is, in the words of our critic Nathan Lee, a “gore-soaked, titty-bouncing, sexploitation fever dream girded by real conceptual brio.” Meditations on the perverse riddles of desire as well as the queer subtexts of many slasher films and the kind of strange identification they invite from the spectator are rendered with perfectly pitched horror theatrics and laugh-out-loud humor.

Film Comment Editor Devika Girish spoke with Schoenbrun about this very rich text, trying to unpack the film’s layers—but not too hard, because if there’s one thing you can take away from Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, it’s that analysis is a boner-killer and mystery is hot.
